issues.description: Abstract reverses the perceived-impact hypothesis: The abstract appears to reverse the perceived-impact extension: it says results supported lower perceived impact when participants faced an identifiable victim or the joint identifiable-plus-statistics condition, whereas the extension rationale and Hypothesis 6 predict higher perceived impact for identifiable than statistical victims. The simulated post-hoc results also do not appear to support the abstract’s wording for the identifiable-vs-statistical contrast; the reported significant difference is between the statistical and joint conditions.
issues.quote: To extend the replication, we added the "perceived impact of donation" as a factor that is believed to be linked with the identifiable victim effect. Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.subcategory: Replication classification seems hard to square with deviations
issues.description: Replication classification seems hard to square with deviations: The classification of the project as a close-to-very-close replication may be somewhat overstated given the document's own deviations. In particular, replacing consequential donation behavior with imaginary donation choices and merging Studies 1 and 3 into a factorial design that applies the intervention to the joint condition may affect core DV/IV structure, not only peripheral stimuli or procedural details.

issues.subcategory: Results section treats simulated data as findings
issues.description: Results section treats simulated data as findings: The Abstract and Results section repeatedly interpret the randomized Qualtrics placeholder output as empirical findings. Although the document flags the data as simulated, statements such as finding no empirical support, participants tending to donate more, and results being contrary to the original study are not supported by randomized pipeline-check data and should remain clearly hypothetical until real data are analyzed.

issues.subcategory: Miscalculated effect sizes (r instead of d) cause CIs to incorrectly include zero
issues.description: Miscalculated effect sizes (r instead of d) cause CIs to incorrectly include zero: The effect-size pipeline in Tables 10 and 14 appears mis-specified. The values labeled as Cohen's $d$ match the point-biserial correlation $r$ computed from the reported $t$ and residual degrees of freedom, and the reported confidence intervals can include zero even when the corresponding Bonferroni-adjusted tests are significant. This should be corrected before applying the pipeline to the actual data.

issues.subcategory: Interaction result is not unpacked by the reported tests
issues.description: Interaction result is not unpacked by the reported tests: The follow-up tests do not fully unpack the reported identifiability-by-intervention interaction. The marginal identifiability post-hocs and the pooled identifiable/no-intervention-versus-five-other-conditions contrast do not isolate the simple effects most relevant to Hypotheses 3 and 4, such as whether the intervention selectively reduces donations within the identifiable condition and not within the statistical condition.
issues.quote:
We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation. Results from Table 9 showed that no significant effect was found on intervention but the
identifiability and the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported.
To further deduce the particular conditions in resulting the above significant findings, we performed post-hoc tests for the difference of identifiability on donation. From Table 10, we noticed that there is a significant difference between identifiable and statistical victim condition, $\mathrm{t}(994)=-2.40, \mathrm{SE}=0.13, \mathrm{p}=.049$, meaning that participants who faced an identifiable victim ( $\mathrm{M}=2.54, \mathrm{SD}=1.76$ ) tended to donate more than those who faced the statistical victims ( $\mathrm{M}=2.24$, $\mathrm{SD}=1.67$ ).

Given the significant interaction effect, we also conducted a t -test to study if the mean of identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

(2007) is an ambitious undertaking, and the use of a dummy dataset to test the analytical pipeline is an excellent step. As you finalize the pre-registration and prepare for data collection, here are several considerations regarding the alignment of the theoretical estimands with the merged experimental design.

**Mapping the merged design to the replication estimands**

Merging Study 1’s explicit deliberation manipulation with Study 3’s joint-presentation manipulation produces an efficient 2 × 3 design, but analyzing all six cells jointly alters the nature of the original replication tests. This structural shift is apparent in the Design section and in Tables 3 and 5, where omnibus tests encompass all conditions. Specifically, changing the key Study 1 contrast from identifiable/no-intervention versus the relevant original cells to identifiable/no-intervention versus the other five conditions transforms the underlying question. Readers will find the replication claim easiest to interpret if the primary original tests are isolated: evaluating Study 1 primarily on the 2 × 2 identifiable/statistical × intervention subset, and evaluating Study 3 on the identifiable/statistical/joint subset without the explicit intervention. The joint-plus-explicit-intervention cells remain highly valuable but could be explicitly designated as extension conditions rather than folded into the confirmatory replication estimands.

**Construct equivalence in the donation procedure**

The original studies relied on consequential prosocial behavior, drawing from real money participants had received and involving perceived sacrifice and mental accounting. The current procedure uses an “imaginary donation” from $0 to $5 on an online MTurk platform, without a prior earning task. Table 6 currently classifies this design facet as "close to very close." Moving from an incentivized behavioral dependent variable to a hypothetical self-report materially changes the psychological situation, which is particularly consequential when studying affective versus deliberative giving. If incentivized donations cannot be implemented, it would be helpful to explicitly frame the study as a conceptual or construct-generalization replication and calibrate the inferential claims accordingly.

**Alignment of the sampling plan and power analysis**

The Participants section powers the study based on the smallest original main-effect estimate ($d = -0.36$), but the decisive inferential tests for this replication are specific interactions, planned contrasts, and Study 3 comparisons within the broader cell design. An overall $N$ justified for a two-group main effect does not secure adequte power for the required difference-in-differences estimates or the cell-to-cell differences (such as the identifiable-versus-joint contrast) after anticipated exclusions. Additionally, Table 4 leaves specific details about the MTurk sample unspecified. The pre-registration would benefit from a cell-level sampling plan tied directly to the primary interaction and contrast tests, mapping the target $N$ per cell after clearly defined attention and data-quality checks.

**Aligning the statistical plan with replication evaluation criteria**

Table 5 centers the analytical plan on 2 × 3 ANOVAs and conditional Bonferroni post-hoc tests, stating that some contrasts will only be conducted if omnibus effects are significant. In a pre-registered replication context, the focal tests should be the planned contrasts corresponding exactly to the original hypotheses, and these should be conducted and reported with effect sizes and confidence intervals regardless of omnibus significance. Furthermore, while the manuscript introduces the LeBel et al. framework, it does not currently operationalize how those specific criteria will be applied to the target estimands (comparing direction, magnitude, and uncertainty). Finally, because the dependent variable is bounded ($0–$5), Small et al. utilized an ordered probit regression. The statistical plan should either reinstate an ordered/bounded-data model or formally justify a comparability analysis alongside robustness checks.

**Situating the perceived-impact extension**

The manuscript discusses perceived impact simultaneously as an added “feeling” item and, as seen in Hypothesis 6, as a theoretical extension with its own directional predictions. Because Tables 3 and 5 do not sharply differentiate it from the central affective mechanism, it is unclear whether perceived impact will be analyzed as part of the original affective composite, a distinct dependent variable, or an exploratory mediator. Given the centrality of affective reactions to the original theoretical model, integrating a new item without a cleanly separated measurement and analysis plan risks contaminating the replication of the original affect findings.
